title: A Bank Holiday Isn't Inefficiency, It's a Fraud Control
dek: When the financial system goes dark on weekends and holidays, it looks like technological backwardness. It's actually a deliberate control: it keeps conspirators from all sitting at the keyboard at once, and that exposes internal fraud.
why: Medium information density, with the core insight concentrated in the middle and later sections: how holidays are used as an anti-fraud control, and why a 24/7 financial system doesn't hold together logically.
who: Engineers and product managers working on payments, clearing and settlement, and cross-border financial infrastructure, plus finance practitioners who care about operational risk and internal control design.
skip: The sponsor read from 15:07 to 18:27 can be skipped.

points.h: Holidays are a Schelling point both sides default to
points.body: A holiday isn't an authoritative list; it's a Schelling point you and your counterparty default to on each other's behalf. Nobody questions that Christmas is a holiday in the US, so nobody has to ask. But a holiday can also be the product of explicit negotiation: one reason government payroll modernization projects keep failing is that it takes a historian doing a great deal of bespoke research to determine which document governs the overtime rate for a Chicago parking enforcement officer on Good Friday. A holiday is both a fact "every child knows" and a negotiable object that can be litigated.

points.h: The Bank of Japan's Company Foundation Day is on no official list
points.body: The Bank of Japan is also a Japanese company, so some of its staffing and computer systems rest on days when most office workers are at work, because that day is the bank's own Company Foundation Day. Institutions that interact with it inherit the counterparty's corporate founding anniversary for certain operations. That holiday appears on no list in government publications, Bloomberg, or Google Calendar, yet it carries all the consequences of a holiday. Once you trip over it, the engineering team has to urgently redefine how the system understands global holidays — because when the system asks "is today a holiday," it usually passes in a jurisdiction but not a counterparty.

points.h: Black Friday falls inside the four days money doesn't move
points.body: Black Friday is the day after Thanksgiving, Cyber Monday follows right behind, and on both days transaction volume spikes as predictably as the sun rising — and they land squarely inside a four-day window in which the banking system largely doesn't move money between companies. If you promise a customer "we'll pay out the next business day" while the underlying rails take two business days to get the money to you, you have a one-day mismatch, and that mismatch consumes float. Normally you only have to front one day; on a weekend you front three; during BFCM you front about five, including the biggest sales day of the year. That's why several hundred people spend weeks in advance walking through BFCM scenarios, writing contingency plans, and modeling float requirements with finance.

points.h: Crypto tried 24/7, and two banks closing at once broke it
points.body: Heavily online technologists hate systems that go down on a predictable schedule, and the crypto world especially loves distributed systems that are always on with no single point of failure. One idea: have every market participant bank at the same bank, get internal APIs for book transfers, and money can move 24/7 — then add a second bank for redundancy. Crypto did try this road, and in 2023 discovered just how questionable the design was when two highly correlated banks closed on adjacent weekends at the same time. The lesson: systems that mediate between cultures are useful, and mediating systems frequently need to bridge gaps in operating schedules — a gap that can't be eliminated by declaring "the only operating schedule is 24/7."

points.h: Forced vacation is meant to keep conspirators from assembling
points.body: Banks deliberately create misaligned operating schedules; it's an important tool for detecting and containing certain kinds of fraud. The most terrifying fraud comes from insiders who know the back-office processes: a single insider who understands the back office is enough to bring down a bank or cause billions in losses — Barings and Daiwa in '95, Société Générale in '08, UBS in '11 are all examples. One very old control is forced vacation, whose purpose is to keep the group involved in a conspiracy from assembling enough co-conspirators, in the right place on the right day, all sitting at the keyboard at once. So a financial CEO sleeping on a beanbag chair in the office may be very dedicated, but the company and he himself had both better not allow it.

points.h: Expecting the financial system to be always on isn't even self-consistent
points.body: In a world that is ever more interconnected, where decision-makers increasingly care about nines, it's reasonable to expect the financial system to partly narrow the gap between historical and contemporary practice. Culture creates systems, and systems create culture; both change, and infrastructure changes far more slowly than fashion, but it does change. Still, expecting the financial system to run continuously isn't just something you shouldn't expect — it isn't even a self-consistent expectation: the financial system is an interconnected network of organizations, systems, and subsystems nested layer upon layer, resting at the bottom on individuals who have been made complex sociocultural promises and who have a physiological need for sleep. These people will keep resting and celebrating periodically, just as they keep working for the society the financial system supports.

quotes.text: A holiday is any day you and your counterparty mutually agree is a holiday.
Guess which holiday none of the above data sources will mention. But it is definitely a holiday , because it has all the consequences of being a holiday .
You need to float five-ish days, including the largest sale day of the year . And you whisper fervent prayers that all the wires you expect arrive exactly when you expect them.

systems which intermediate between cultures are useful . Intermediating between cultures is a thing the world urgently needs and is extremely prepared to pay for . Systems which intermediate between cultures will frequently need to cross a gap between operating schedules. You cannot simply wish away that gap.

A very old control for this sort of thing is forcing holidays, with the goal that the set of staff engaged in a conspiracy don't have a sufficient number of conspirators at the keyboard, in all the right places, on all the right days, the conspiracy needs to operate to be undetected.

If we didn't have holidays, we'd have been forced to invent them. We accept degraded performance (very useful humans: not at keyboard!) as an organizational chaos monkey to shake out far more serious issues.
But should one expect the financial system to operate constantly? Not only should you not expect that, that is not even a coherent thing to expect.
